title: Mapping
content:
Let $A$ and $B$ be nonempty sets. A mapping (or
function) $F:A \to B$ is a rule that assigns to each
element $a \in A$ a unique element $F(a) \in B$. The set
$A$ is called the domain of $F$, and $B$ is called the
codomain. For $a \in A$, the element $F(a) \in B$ is called
the image of $a$, and $a$ is called a preimage of
$F(a)$. The set of all images,
$\{F(a) : a \in A\} \subseteq B$, is called the range of
$F$.

title: Example 4.1 --- Identifying Domain Codomain and Range
content:
Let $F:\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be defined by $F(x)=x^2$. Identify
the domain, codomain, and range of $F$.

Solution:
The domain is $\mathbb{R}$ (all real inputs are allowed), and the
codomain is $\mathbb{R}$ (as stated in the definition of $F$).

Since $x^2 \ge 0$ for every real $x$, and every nonnegative real
number $y$ has a preimage ($x=\sqrt{y}$), the range consists of all
nonnegative reals:
\[
\text{Domain} = \boxed{\mathbb{R}}, \qquad \text{Codomain} =
\boxed{\mathbb{R}}, \qquad \text{Range} = \boxed{[0,\infty)}
\]

\bigskip

title: Example 4.2 --- A Mapping Between Vector Spaces
content:
Let $F:\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ be defined by
$F(x,y)=(x+y,\ x-y,\ 2x)$. Find $F(3,1)$.

Solution:
Substitute $x=3$, $y=1$ into each component:
$$$$\begin{align*}
x+y &= 3+1 = 4\\
x-y &= 3-1 = 2\\
2x &= 2(3) = 6
\end{align*}$$$$
\[
F(3,1) = \boxed{(4,\ 2,\ 6)}
\]

\bigskip

title: Example 4.3 --- Checking Whether a Rule Is a Mapping
content:
Determine whether $F:\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by
$F(x,y)=\dfrac{1}{x-y}$ is a mapping on all of $\mathbb{R}^2$.

Solution:
For $F$ to be a mapping on the full domain $\mathbb{R}^2$, every
element $(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2$ must produce a unique well-defined
output.

Consider $(x,y)=(2,2)$. Then $F(2,2)=\dfrac{1}{2-2}=\dfrac{1}{0}$,
which is undefined.

Since not every element of $\mathbb{R}^2$ has a defined image, $F$
is not a mapping on all of $\mathbb{R}^2$; its actual
domain is restricted to $\{(x,y) : x \neq y\}$. \hfill$\square$

title: {Types of Mappings:} {enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] {Injective (one-to-one):}
content:
Types of Mappings:

1. Injective (one-to-one): $F(a_1)=F(a_2) \implies
        a_1=a_2$ --- distinct inputs give distinct outputs.
2. Surjective (onto): every $b \in B$ has at least one
        preimage --- the range equals the codomain.
3. Bijective: both injective and surjective ---
        every element of $B$ has exactly one preimage.
4. Composition: if $F:A \to B$ and $G:B \to C$, the
        composition $G \circ F: A \to C$ is defined by
        $(G \circ F)(a)=G(F(a))$.

title: Linear Mapping (Linear Transformation)
content:
Let $V$ and $U$ be vector spaces over the same field $K$. A mapping
$F:V \to U$ is called a linear mapping (or linear
transformation) if it satisfies the following two conditions for
all $v_1,v_2 \in V$ and all $k \in K$:

1. $F(v_1+v_2) = F(v_1)+F(v_2)$ \hfill (additivity)
2. $F(kv_1) = kF(v_1)$ \hfill (homogeneity)

Equivalently, $F$ is linear if and only if for all
$v_1,v_2 \in V$ and $a,b \in K$:
\[
F(av_1+bv_2) = aF(v_1)+bF(v_2).
\]
Every linear mapping satisfies $F(0)=0$.

title: Example 4.4 --- Verifying a Linear Mapping
content:
Show that $F:\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ defined by
$F(x,y,z)=(2x-y,\ y+3z)$ is a linear mapping.

Solution:
Let $u=(x_1,y_1,z_1)$ and $v=(x_2,y_2,z_2)$ be arbitrary vectors in
$\mathbb{R}^3$, and let $a,b \in \mathbb{R}$.

Compute $F(au+bv)$:
$$$$\begin{align*}
au+bv &= (ax_1+bx_2,\ ay_1+by_2,\ az_1+bz_2)\\
F(au+bv) &= \big(2(ax_1+bx_2)-(ay_1+by_2),\ (ay_1+by_2)+3(az_1+bz_2)\big)\\
&= \big(a(2x_1-y_1)+b(2x_2-y_2),\ a(y_1+3z_1)+b(y_2+3z_2)\big).
\end{align*}$$$$

Compute $aF(u)+bF(v)$:
$$$$\begin{align*}
aF(u)+bF(v) &= a(2x_1-y_1,\ y_1+3z_1)+b(2x_2-y_2,\ y_2+3z_2)\\
&= \big(a(2x_1-y_1)+b(2x_2-y_2),\ a(y_1+3z_1)+b(y_2+3z_2)\big).
\end{align*}$$$$

Since $F(au+bv)=aF(u)+bF(v)$ for arbitrary $u,v,a,b$, $F$ is a
linear mapping. \hfill$\square$

\bigskip

title: Example 4.5 --- A Mapping That Is Not Linear
content:
Show that $F:\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ defined by
$F(x,y)=(x^2,\ y)$ is not a linear mapping.

Solution:
It suffices to find one instance where homogeneity or additivity
fails. Test homogeneity with $k=2$ and $v=(1,1)$:
\[
F(kv) = F(2,2) = (2^2,\ 2) = (4,2).
\]
\[
kF(v) = 2F(1,1) = 2(1^2,\ 1) = 2(1,1) = (2,2).
\]
Since $F(kv)=(4,2) \neq (2,2)=kF(v)$, the homogeneity condition
fails.

Therefore $F$ is not a linear mapping. \hfill$\square$

\bigskip

title: Example 4.6 --- The Zero Mapping and Identity Mapping
content:
Show that the zero mapping $F:V \to U$ defined by $F(v)=0$ for all
$v \in V$, and the identity mapping $I:V \to V$ defined by
$I(v)=v$, are both linear mappings.

Solution:
Zero mapping: For any $v_1,v_2 \in V$ and $a,b \in K$:
\[
F(av_1+bv_2) = 0 = a(0)+b(0) = aF(v_1)+bF(v_2).
\]
So $F$ is linear.

Identity mapping: For any $v_1,v_2 \in V$ and $a,b \in K$:
\[
I(av_1+bv_2) = av_1+bv_2 = aI(v_1)+bI(v_2).
\]
So $I$ is linear. \hfill$\square$

\bigskip

title: Example 4.7 --- Linear Mapping Defined by a Matrix
content:
Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&-1\\3&1\end{bmatrix}$, and define
$F:\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ by $F(v)=Av$ (treating $v$ as a
column vector). Find $F(2,-3)$ and confirm $F$ is linear.

Solution:
\[
F(2,-3) = \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&-1\\3&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2\\-3\end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix}1(2)+2(-3)\\0(2)+(-1)(-3)\\3(2)+1(-3)\end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix}-4\\3\\3\end{bmatrix}
\]
\[
F(2,-3) = \boxed{(-4,\ 3,\ 3)}
\]

To confirm linearity: for any vectors $u,v \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and
scalars $a,b$, matrix multiplication satisfies
$A(au+bv)=aAu+bAv$ by the distributive and associative properties
of matrix algebra. Hence $F(au+bv)=aF(u)+bF(v)$, confirming $F$ is
linear. In fact, every mapping of the form $F(v)=Av$ for a
fixed matrix $A$ is automatically linear. \hfill$\square$

title: Properties of Linear Mappings
content:
1. $F(0) = 0$ for every linear mapping $F$ \hfill (zero preservation)
2. $F(-v) = -F(v)$ for all $v \in V$ \hfill (negative preservation)
3. If $F,G:V \to U$ are linear, then $F+G$ and $kF$ are also
        linear \hfill (closure under operations)
4. If $F:V \to U$ and $G:U \to W$ are linear, then
        $G \circ F: V \to W$ is linear \hfill (composition)
5. $F$ is completely determined by its action on a basis: if
        $F(u_1),\dots,F(u_n)$ are known for a basis
        $\{u_1,\dots,u_n\}$ of $V$, then $F(v)$ is known for every
        $v \in V$ \hfill (basis determination)

title: Example 4.8 --- Determining F from Its Action on a Basis
{Testing Whether a Mapping Is Linear
content:
Testing Whether a Mapping Is Linear --- Exam Strategy:

1. Every component of $F(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ must be a
        linear expression in $x_1,\dots,x_n$ (no squares,
        products of variables, constants added, or other
        nonlinear terms).
2. A quick necessary check: if $F(0) \neq 0$, then $F$ is
        immediately not linear.
3. Any mapping of the form $F(v)=Av$ for a fixed matrix $A$ is
        automatically linear.
4. To disprove linearity, one specific counterexample (failing
        additivity or homogeneity) is sufficient.

section: Kernel and Image of a Linear Mapping
title: Kernel and Image
content:
Let $F:V \to U$ be a linear mapping. The kernel of $F$,
denoted $\ker(F)$, is the set of all vectors in $V$ that map to the
zero vector of $U$:
\[
\ker(F) = \{v \in V : F(v) = 0\}.
\]
The image of $F$, denoted $\operatorname{Im}(F)$, is the
set of all vectors in $U$ that are images of some vector in $V$:
\[
\operatorname{Im}(F) = \{F(v) : v \in V\}.
\]
Both $\ker(F)$ and $\operatorname{Im}(F)$ are subspaces --- $\ker(F)$
is a subspace of $V$, and $\operatorname{Im}(F)$ is a subspace of
$U$. The dimension of $\ker(F)$ is called the nullity of
$F$, and the dimension of $\operatorname{Im}(F)$ is called the
rank of $F$.

section: Kernel and Image of a Linear Mapping
title: Example 4.9 --- Finding the Kernel of a Linear Mapping
content:
Let $F:\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be defined by
$F(x,y,z)=(x+y+z,\ x-y-z)$. Find $\ker(F)$.

Solution:
We need all $(x,y,z)$ such that $F(x,y,z)=(0,0)$:
$$$$\begin{align*}
x+y+z &= 0\\
x-y-z &= 0
\end{align*}$$$$
Adding the two equations: $2x=0 \implies x=0$. Substituting into
the first equation: $y+z=0 \implies y=-z$.

So every vector in $\ker(F)$ has the form $(0,-z,z)=z(0,-1,1)$ for
$z \in \mathbb{R}$.
\[
\ker(F) = \boxed{\operatorname{span}\{(0,-1,1)\}}, \qquad
\text{nullity}(F) = 1
\]

\bigskip

section: Kernel and Image of a Linear Mapping
title: Example 4.10 --- Finding the Image of a Linear Mapping
content:
Let $F:\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ be defined by
$F(x,y,z)=(x+y,\ y+z,\ x+2y+z)$. Find $\operatorname{Im}(F)$.

Solution:
Write $F(x,y,z)$ as a linear combination of vectors formed from the
coefficients of $x$, $y$, $z$:
\[
F(x,y,z) = x(1,0,1)+y(1,1,2)+z(0,1,1).
\]
So $\operatorname{Im}(F) = \operatorname{span}\{(1,0,1),(1,1,2),(0,1,1)\}$.
Check for dependence: is $(1,1,2)=a(1,0,1)+b(0,1,1)$?
$$$$\begin{align*}
a &= 1\\
b &= 1\\
a+b &= 1+1 = 2 \quad \checkmark
\end{align*}$$$$
Since $(1,1,2)=(1,0,1)+(0,1,1)$, the third spanning vector is
redundant. A basis for $\operatorname{Im}(F)$ is
$\{(1,0,1),(0,1,1)\}$, which are independent (not proportional).
\[
\operatorname{Im}(F) = \boxed{\operatorname{span}\{(1,0,1),(0,1,1)\}}, \qquad
\text{rank}(F) = 2
\]

\bigskip

section: Kernel and Image of a Linear Mapping
title: Example 4.11 --- Verifying the Kernel Is a Subspace
content:
Let $F:V \to U$ be a linear mapping. Prove that $\ker(F)$ is a
subspace of $V$.

Solution:
Zero vector: Since $F$ is linear, $F(0)=0$, so
$0 \in \ker(F)$. ✓

Closure under addition: Let $v_1,v_2 \in \ker(F)$, so
$F(v_1)=0$ and $F(v_2)=0$. Then
\[
F(v_1+v_2) = F(v_1)+F(v_2) = 0+0 = 0,
\]
so $v_1+v_2 \in \ker(F)$. ✓

Closure under scalar multiplication: Let $v \in \ker(F)$
and $k \in K$. Then
\[
F(kv) = kF(v) = k(0) = 0,
\]
so $kv \in \ker(F)$. ✓

All three subspace conditions hold, so $\ker(F)$ is a subspace of
$V$. \hfill$\square$

section: Kernel and Image of a Linear Mapping
title: Rank-Nullity Theorem
content:
Let $F:V \to U$ be a linear mapping, where $V$ is
finite-dimensional. Then:
\[
\dim(V) = \dim(\ker(F)) + \dim(\operatorname{Im}(F)),
\]
that is,
\[
\dim(V) = \text{nullity}(F) + \text{rank}(F).
\]

section: Kernel and Image of a Linear Mapping
title: Example 4.12 --- Applying the Rank-Nullity Theorem
content:
Let $F:\mathbb{R}^4 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ be a linear mapping with
$\dim(\ker(F))=2$. Find $\text{rank}(F)$.

Solution:
By the Rank-Nullity Theorem:
\[
\dim(\mathbb{R}^4) = \text{nullity}(F)+\text{rank}(F).
\]
\[
4 = 2 + \text{rank}(F) \implies \text{rank}(F) = 2.
\]
\[
\text{rank}(F) = \boxed{2}
\]

\bigskip

section: Kernel and Image of a Linear Mapping
title: Example 4.13 --- Kernel and Rank-Nullity Verification
content:
Let $F:\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be defined by
$F(x,y,z)=(2x-y+z,\ x+y-z)$. Find $\ker(F)$, $\operatorname{Im}(F)$,
and verify the Rank-Nullity Theorem.

Solution:
Kernel: solve $2x-y+z=0$ and $x+y-z=0$ simultaneously.
Adding: $3x=0 \implies x=0$. Then from the second equation,
$y=z$. So $\ker(F)=\{(0,z,z)\} = \operatorname{span}\{(0,1,1)\}$,
giving $\text{nullity}(F)=1$.

Image: write
\[
F(x,y,z) = x(2,1)+y(-1,1)+z(1,-1).
\]
Since $(1,-1)=-1(-1,1)$, the third vector is redundant. Also
$(2,1)$ and $(-1,1)$ are independent (not proportional). So
$\operatorname{Im}(F)=\operatorname{span}\{(2,1),(-1,1)\}$. Since
these two vectors are independent in $\mathbb{R}^2$, they span all
of $\mathbb{R}^2$, giving $\text{rank}(F)=2$.

Verification:
\[
\text{nullity}(F)+\text{rank}(F) = 1+2 = 3 = \dim(\mathbb{R}^3). \quad\checkmark
\]
\hfill$\square$

title: Nonsingular Linear Mapping and Isomorphism
content:
A linear mapping $F:V \to U$ is called nonsingular if
$\ker(F)=\{0\}$; otherwise, $F$ is called singular. A
nonsingular linear mapping is always injective
(one-to-one).

If $F:V \to U$ is linear, bijective (both injective and
surjective), then $F$ is called an isomorphism, and $V$ and
$U$ are said to be isomorphic, written $V \cong U$. Two
finite-dimensional vector spaces over the same field are isomorphic
if and only if they have the same dimension.

title: Example 4.14 --- Testing for Nonsingularity
content:
Determine whether $F:\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ defined by
$F(x,y,z)=(x+y,\ y+z,\ x+z)$ is nonsingular.

Solution:
Find $\ker(F)$ by solving $F(x,y,z)=(0,0,0)$:
$$$$\begin{align*}
x+y &= 0 \tag{1}\\
y+z &= 0 \tag{2}\\
x+z &= 0 \tag{3}
\end{align*}$$$$
From (1): $y=-x$. From (2): $z=-y=x$. Check (3): $x+z=x+x=2x=0
\implies x=0$. Then $y=0$, $z=0$.

Since the only solution is $(0,0,0)$, $\ker(F)=\{0\}$. Hence $F$ is
nonsingular. \hfill$\square$

\bigskip

title: Example 4.15 --- Testing for Singularity
content:
Determine whether $F:\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ defined by
$F(x,y,z)=(x+y+z,\ 2x+2y+2z)$ is singular or nonsingular.

Solution:
Find $\ker(F)$: solve $x+y+z=0$ and $2x+2y+2z=0$. The second
equation is exactly twice the first, so they represent the same
condition: $x+y+z=0$.

This single equation has infinitely many solutions, e.g.
$(1,-1,0) \neq (0,0,0)$ satisfies $F(1,-1,0)=(0,0)$.

Since $\ker(F) \neq \{0\}$, $F$ is singular. \hfill$\square$

\bigskip

title: Example 4.16 --- Verifying an Isomorphism
content:
Let $F:\mathbb{R}^2 \to P_1(t)$ be defined by
$F(a,b) = a+bt$. Show that $F$ is an isomorphism.

Solution:
Linearity: for $(a_1,b_1),(a_2,b_2) \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and
scalars $c_1,c_2$:
$$$$\begin{align*}
F\big(c_1(a_1,b_1)+c_2(a_2,b_2)\big)
&= F(c_1a_1+c_2a_2,\ c_1b_1+c_2b_2)\\
&= (c_1a_1+c_2a_2)+(c_1b_1+c_2b_2)t\\
&= c_1(a_1+b_1t)+c_2(a_2+b_2t)\\
&= c_1F(a_1,b_1)+c_2F(a_2,b_2).
\end{align*}$$$$
So $F$ is linear.

Nonsingular (injective): if $F(a,b)=0$, then $a+bt=0$,
which forces $a=0$ and $b=0$ (a polynomial is zero only when all
coefficients are zero). So $\ker(F)=\{(0,0)\}$, and $F$ is
nonsingular, hence injective.

Surjective: every polynomial $p(t)=a+bt \in P_1(t)$ is the
image of $(a,b) \in \mathbb{R}^2$, since $F(a,b)=a+bt=p(t)$.

Since $F$ is linear, injective, and surjective, $F$ is an
isomorphism, so $\mathbb{R}^2 \cong P_1(t)$. This agrees
with the fact that $\dim(\mathbb{R}^2)=2=\dim(P_1(t))$. \hfill$\square$

title: Properties of Nonsingular Mappings and Isomorphisms
content:
1. $F$ is nonsingular if and only if $F$ is injective \hfill (injectivity criterion)
2. If $\dim(V)=\dim(U)$, then $F:V \to U$ is nonsingular if and
        only if $F$ is an isomorphism \hfill (equal-dimension shortcut)
3. If $F:V \to U$ is nonsingular and
        $\{v_1,\dots,v_n\}$ is linearly independent in $V$, then
        $\{F(v_1),\dots,F(v_n)\}$ is linearly independent in $U$ \hfill (independence preservation)
4. Every $n$-dimensional vector space over $K$ is isomorphic to
        $K^n$ \hfill (coordinate isomorphism)
5. The inverse of an isomorphism $F:V \to U$ is also an
        isomorphism $F^{-1}:U \to V$ \hfill (inverse property)

title: {Kernel Rank-Nullity --- Exam Strategy:} {enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
content:
Kernel Rank-Nullity --- Exam Strategy:

1. To find $\ker(F)$: set $F(v)=0$ and solve the resulting
        homogeneous system.
2. To find $\operatorname{Im}(F)$: write $F(v)$ as a linear
        combination of vectors formed from the coefficients, then
        reduce the spanning set to a basis.
3. Use $\dim(V)=\text{nullity}(F)+\text{rank}(F)$ to check work
        or shortcut a computation once one of the two dimensions is
        known.
4. $F$ nonsingular $\iff$ $\ker(F)=\{0\}$ $\iff$ $F$ injective
        $\iff$ nullity$(F)=0$.

title: Operations on Linear Mappings
content:
Let $F,G:V \to U$ be linear mappings and $k$ a scalar. The
sum $F+G$ and scalar multiple $kF$ are the
mappings $V \to U$ defined by:
\[
(F+G)(v) = F(v)+G(v), \qquad (kF)(v) = kF(v) \quad \text{for all } v \in V.
\]
If $F:V \to U$ and $G:U \to W$ are linear, the composition
$G \circ F: V \to W$ is defined by
\[
(G \circ F)(v) = G(F(v)) \quad \text{for all } v \in V.
\]
The set of all linear mappings from $V$ to $U$, denoted
$\operatorname{Hom}(V,U)$, is itself a vector space under the sum
and scalar multiple defined above.

title: Example 4.17 --- Sum and Scalar Multiple of Linear Mappings
content:
Let $F,G:\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be defined by
$F(x,y)=(x+y,\ x)$ and $G(x,y)=(2x,\ y-x)$. Find $(F+G)(x,y)$ and
$(3F)(x,y)$.

Solution:
$$$$\begin{align*}
(F+G)(x,y) &= F(x,y)+G(x,y) = (x+y,\ x)+(2x,\ y-x)\\
&= (x+y+2x,\ x+y-x) = (3x+y,\ y).
\end{align*}$$$$
\[
(3F)(x,y) = 3(x+y,\ x) = (3x+3y,\ 3x)
\]
\[
(F+G)(x,y) = \boxed{(3x+y,\ y)}, \qquad (3F)(x,y) = \boxed{(3x+3y,\ 3x)}
\]

\bigskip

title: Example 4.18 --- Composition of Linear Mappings
content:
Let $F,G:\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be defined by
$F(x,y)=(x+y,\ x-y)$ and $G(x,y)=(2x,\ 3y)$. Find $(G \circ F)(x,y)$.

Solution:
\[
(G \circ F)(x,y) = G\big(F(x,y)\big) = G(x+y,\ x-y).
\]
Substitute into $G$, replacing its first argument by $x+y$ and its
second by $x-y$:
\[
G(x+y,\ x-y) = \big(2(x+y),\ 3(x-y)\big) = (2x+2y,\ 3x-3y).
\]
\[
(G \circ F)(x,y) = \boxed{(2x+2y,\ 3x-3y)}
\]

\bigskip

title: Example 4.19 --- Proving F+G Is Linear
content:
Let $F,G:V \to U$ be linear mappings. Prove that $F+G$ is also a
linear mapping.

Solution:
Let $v_1,v_2 \in V$ and $a,b \in K$. By definition of $F+G$ and the
linearity of $F$ and $G$ separately:
$$$$\begin{align*}
(F+G)(av_1+bv_2) &= F(av_1+bv_2)+G(av_1+bv_2)\\
&= \big(aF(v_1)+bF(v_2)\big)+\big(aG(v_1)+bG(v_2)\big)\\
&= a\big(F(v_1)+G(v_1)\big)+b\big(F(v_2)+G(v_2)\big)\\
&= a(F+G)(v_1)+b(F+G)(v_2).
\end{align*}$$$$
Since $(F+G)(av_1+bv_2)=a(F+G)(v_1)+b(F+G)(v_2)$ for arbitrary
$v_1,v_2,a,b$, the mapping $F+G$ is linear. \hfill$\square$

title: Properties of the Space of Linear Mappings
content:
1. $\operatorname{Hom}(V,U)$ is a vector space under $+$ and
        scalar multiplication \hfill (vector space structure)
2. If $\dim(V)=m$ and $\dim(U)=n$, then
        $\dim(\operatorname{Hom}(V,U))=mn$ \hfill (dimension formula)
3. Composition distributes over addition:
        $G\circ(F_1+F_2)=G\circ F_1+G\circ F_2$ \hfill (distributivity)
4. Composition is associative:
        $(H\circ G)\circ F = H\circ(G\circ F)$ \hfill (associativity)
5. Composition is generally not commutative:
        $G\circ F \neq F\circ G$ in general \hfill (non-commutativity)

title: Linear Operator and the Algebra A(V)
content:
A linear mapping $F:V \to V$ (same domain and codomain) is called a
linear operator on $V$. The set of all linear operators on
$V$, denoted $A(V)$, forms an algebra: it is a vector space
under $+$ and scalar multiplication, and it is also closed under
composition, which plays the role of multiplication. For
$F,G \in A(V)$, the product $FG$ means $F \circ G$. Powers are
defined by $F^2=F\circ F$, $F^n=F\circ F \circ \cdots \circ F$
($n$ times), and $F^0=I$ (the identity operator). For a polynomial
$p(t)=a_0+a_1t+\cdots+a_nt^n$, the operator
\[
p(F) = a_0I+a_1F+a_2F^2+\cdots+a_nF^n
\]
is called a polynomial in the operator $F$. An operator $F$
is invertible if there exists $G \in A(V)$ with $FG=GF=I$;
this $G$ is denoted $F^{-1}$.

title: Example 4.20 --- Computing Powers of a Linear Operator
content:
Let $F:\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be defined by
$F(x,y)=(y,\ -x)$. Find $F^2(x,y)$ and identify the operator
$F^2$.

Solution:
$$$$\begin{align*}
F^2(x,y) &= F\big(F(x,y)\big) = F(y,-x)\\
&= (-x,\ -y) = -1(x,y).
\end{align*}$$$$
Since $F^2(x,y)=-(x,y)$ for every $(x,y)$, the operator $F^2$ is
simply $-1$ times the identity operator:
\[
F^2 = \boxed{-I}
\]

\bigskip

title: Example 4.21 --- Testing Invertibility of an Operator
content:
Let $F:\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be defined by
$F(x,y)=(x+y,\ x-y)$. Show that $F$ is invertible and find
$F^{-1}$.

Solution:
Nonsingularity: solve $x+y=0$ and $x-y=0$. Adding gives
$2x=0 \implies x=0$, and then $y=0$. So $\ker(F)=\{0\}$, hence $F$
is nonsingular. Since $F$ maps $\mathbb{R}^2$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$
(same dimension), $F$ is invertible.

Finding $F^{-1}$: let $u=x+y$ and $v=x-y$. Adding these:
$u+v=2x \implies x=\dfrac{u+v}{2}$. Subtracting: $u-v=2y \implies
y=\dfrac{u-v}{2}$.
\[
F^{-1}(u,v) = \boxed{\left(\frac{u+v}{2},\ \frac{u-v}{2}\right)}
\]

\bigskip

title: Example 4.22 --- Evaluating a Polynomial in an Operator
content:
Let $F:\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be defined by
$F(x,y)=(y,\ x)$ (coordinate swap), and let $p(t)=t^2-1$. Compute
$p(F)$.

Solution:
First compute $F^2$:
\[
F^2(x,y) = F\big(F(x,y)\big) = F(y,x) = (x,y).
\]
So $F^2=I$, the identity operator.

Now evaluate $p(F)=F^2-I$:
\[
p(F)(x,y) = F^2(x,y)-I(x,y) = (x,y)-(x,y) = (0,0).
\]
Since $p(F)$ sends every vector to $(0,0)$, $p(F)$ is the
zero operator:
\[
p(F) = \boxed{0}
\]
This shows $F$ is a ``zero'' of the polynomial $p(t)=t^2-1$, in the
same sense that a matrix can be a zero of a polynomial.
\hfill$\square$

title: Properties of the Algebra A(V)
content:
1. $A(V)$ is closed under $+$, scalar multiplication, and
        composition \hfill (closure)
2. The identity operator $I$ satisfies $FI=IF=F$ for all
        $F \in A(V)$ \hfill (multiplicative identity)
3. $F \in A(V)$ is invertible if and only if $F$ is
        nonsingular (equivalently, bijective) \hfill (invertibility criterion)
4. Composition in $A(V)$ is associative but generally
        not commutative: $FG \neq GF$ in general \hfill (non-commutativity)
5. If $F$ is invertible, then $(F^{-1})^{-1}=F$ and
        $(FG)^{-1}=G^{-1}F^{-1}$ \hfill (inverse properties)

title: Matrix Representation of a Linear Mapping
content:
Let $F:V \to U$ be a linear mapping, and let $S=\{v_1,\dots,v_n\}$
and $T=\{u_1,\dots,u_m\}$ be bases of $V$ and $U$ respectively. For
each $v_j$, express $F(v_j)$ as a linear combination of the basis
$T$:
\[
F(v_j) = a_{1j}u_1+a_{2j}u_2+\cdots+a_{mj}u_m.
\]
The $m \times n$ matrix $A=[a_{ij}]$, whose $j$-th column is the
coordinate vector $[F(v_j)]_T$, is called the matrix
representation of $F$ relative to the bases $S$ and $T$, denoted
$[F]_{S,T}$ (or simply $[F]_S$ when $V=U$ and $S=T$). This matrix
satisfies the key property:
\[
[F(v)]_T = [F]_{S,T}\,[v]_S \qquad \text{for every } v \in V.
\]

title: Example 4.23 --- Matrix Representation Relative to Standard Bases
content:
Let $F:\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be defined by
$F(x,y,z)=(2x-y+z,\ x+3y-z)$. Find the matrix representation of
$F$ relative to the standard bases.

Solution:
Apply $F$ to each standard basis vector of $\mathbb{R}^3$:
$$$$\begin{align*}
F(1,0,0) &= (2,1)\\
F(0,1,0) &= (-1,3)\\
F(0,0,1) &= (1,-1)
\end{align*}$$$$
Using these images as the columns of the matrix:
\[
[F] = \boxed{\begin{bmatrix}2&-1&1\\1&3&-1\end{bmatrix}}
\]

\bigskip

title: Example 4.24 --- Matrix Representation Relative to a Nonstandard Basis
content:
Let $F:\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be defined by
$F(x,y)=(x+y,\ x-y)$. Find the matrix representation of $F$
relative to the basis $S=\{(1,1),(1,-1)\}$.

Solution:
Image of $(1,1)$: $F(1,1)=(1+1,\ 1-1)=(2,0)$. Express
$(2,0)$ in terms of $S$: $a(1,1)+b(1,-1)=(2,0)$ gives $a+b=2$,
$a-b=0$, so $a=1$, $b=1$. Coordinate vector: $(1,1)$.

Image of $(1,-1)$: $F(1,-1)=(1-1,\ 1+1)=(0,2)$. Express
$(0,2)$ in terms of $S$: $a+b=0$, $a-b=2$, so $a=1$, $b=-1$.
Coordinate vector: $(1,-1)$.

Using these coordinate vectors as columns:
\[
[F]_S = \boxed{\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}}
\]

\bigskip

title: Example 4.25 --- Using the Matrix Representation to Compute F(v)
content:
Using the mapping and basis $S$ from Example 4.24, let $v=(3,-1)$
with coordinate vector $[v]_S=(1,2)$. Verify that
$[F(v)]_S=[F]_S\,[v]_S$.

Solution:
Direct computation: $F(3,-1) = (3+(-1),\ 3-(-1)) = (2,4)$.
Express $(2,4)$ in terms of $S$: $a+b=2$, $a-b=4$, so $a=3$,
$b=-1$. Thus $[F(v)]_S=(3,-1)$.

Matrix computation:
\[
[F]_S\,[v]_S = \begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix}1(1)+1(2)\\1(1)-1(2)\end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix}3\\-1\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Both methods give $(3,-1)$, confirming
$[F(v)]_S=[F]_S\,[v]_S$. ✓ \hfill$\square$

title: {Matrix Representation --- Key Facts:} {enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
content:
Matrix Representation --- Key Facts:

1. Relative to the standard basis, the matrix
        representation of $F(v)=Av$ is simply $A$ itself.
2. The columns of $[F]_{S,T}$ are the coordinate vectors (with
        respect to $T$) of $F$ applied to each vector of $S$, in
        order.
3. Composition corresponds to matrix multiplication:
        $[G\circ F]_S = [G]_S[F]_S$.
4. $F$ is invertible if and only if $[F]_S$ is an invertible
        matrix, and then $[F^{-1}]_S = ([F]_S)^{-1}$.

title: Practice Problem 1
content:
Let $G:\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be defined by
  $G(x,y,z)=(2x-z,\ y+3z)$. Determine whether $G$ is injective,
  surjective, both, or neither.

title: Practice Problem 2
content:
Let $H:\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be defined by
  $H(x)=\dfrac{2}{x^2-4}$. Determine the largest possible domain of
  $H$ as a subset of $\mathbb{R}$.

title: Practice Problem 3
content:
Let $F,G:\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be defined by
  $F(x,y)=(x+2y,\ 3x-y)$ and $G(x,y)=(y,\ x+y)$. Find
  $(G \circ F)(1,-2)$ and $(F \circ G)(1,-2)$, and comment on
  whether $G \circ F = F \circ G$.

title: Practice Problem 4
content:
Determine whether $F:\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ defined
  by $F(x,y,z)=(x+2y-z,\ 3)$ is a linear mapping.

title: Practice Problem 5
content:
Determine whether $F:M_{2,2} \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by
  $F(A)=\det(A)$ is a linear mapping.

title: Practice Problem 7
content:
Let $F:\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ be defined by
  $F(x,y,z)=(x-y,\ y-z,\ z-x)$. Find $\ker(F)$ and
  $\operatorname{Im}(F)$, and verify the Rank-Nullity Theorem.

title: Practice Problem 8
content:
Let $F:\mathbb{R}^4 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ be defined by
  $F(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)=(x_1+x_2,\ x_2+x_3,\ x_3+x_4)$. Find a basis
  for $\ker(F)$.

title: Practice Problem 9
content:
Let $F:\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be a linear mapping
  with $\operatorname{rank}(F)=2$. Find $\dim(\ker(F))$.

title: Practice Problem 10
content:
Let $F:P_2(t) \to P_1(t)$ be defined by
  $F(a_0+a_1t+a_2t^2)=a_1+2a_2t$. Find $\ker(F)$ and
  $\operatorname{Im}(F)$.

title: Practice Problem 11
content:
Determine whether $F:\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ defined
  by $F(x,y,z)=(x+y,\ y+z,\ x+2y+z)$ is singular or nonsingular.

title: Practice Problem 12
content:
Determine whether $F:\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ defined
  by $F(x,y)=(3x-y,\ x+2y)$ is an isomorphism. If so find
  $F^{-1}$.

title: Practice Problem 13
content:
Show that $M_{2,2}$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^4$ by
  exhibiting an explicit isomorphism.

title: Practice Problem 14
content:
Let $F,G:\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be defined by
  $F(x,y,z)=(x-z,\ 2y)$ and $G(x,y,z)=(x+y,\ z-y)$. Find
  $(2F-3G)(x,y,z)$.

title: Practice Problem 15
content:
Let $F:\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ and
  $G:\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be defined by
  $F(x,y)=(x,\ x+y,\ y)$ and $G(x,y,z)=(x-z,\ y)$. Find
  $(G \circ F)(x,y)$ and determine whether $G \circ F$ is the
  identity mapping on $\mathbb{R}^2$.

title: Practice Problem 16
content:
Prove that if $F:V \to U$ is a linear mapping and $k$ is a
  scalar, then $kF$ is also a linear mapping.

title: Practice Problem 17
content:
Let $F:\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ be defined by
  $F(x,y,z)=(z,\ x,\ y)$. Find $F^2$ and $F^3$, and determine
  whether $F$ is invertible.

title: Practice Problem 18
content:
Let $F:\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be defined by
  $F(x,y)=(2x,\ 3y)$. Show that $F$ is invertible and find
  $F^{-1}$.

title: Practice Problem 19
content:
Let $F:\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be defined by
  $F(x,y)=(-x,\ y)$. Show that $F$ is a zero of the polynomial
  $p(t)=t^2-1$ by computing $p(F)=F^2-I$.

title: Practice Problem 20
content:
Let $F,G$ be linear operators on $\mathbb{R}^2$ defined by
  $F(x,y)=(y,0)$ and $G(x,y)=(0,x)$. Compute $FG$ and $GF$, and
  determine whether $FG=GF$.

title: Practice Problem 21
content:
Find the matrix representation of
  $F:\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ defined by
  $F(x,y,z)=(3x-y+2z,\ x+4z)$ relative to the standard bases.

title: Practice Problem 22
content:
Let $F:\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be defined by
  $F(x,y)=(2x-y,\ x+y)$. Find the matrix representation of $F$
  relative to the basis $S=\{(1,2),(2,3)\}$.

title: Practice Problem 23
content:
Let $F:\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ have matrix
  representation $[F]_S=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&-1\end{bmatrix}$
  relative to a basis $S=\{u_1,u_2\}$. Given that a vector $v$ has
  coordinate vector $[v]_S=(3,-2)$, find $[F(v)]_S$.

title: Practice Problem 24
content:
Let $F:\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ be defined by
  $F(x,y,z)=(x+y+z,\ 2x+ky+2z,\ x+y+z)$. Find all values of $k$
  for which $F$ is singular.

title: Practice Problem 25
content:
Let $F:P_1(t) \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be defined by
  $F(a+bt)=(a-b,\ a+b)$. Show that $F$ is an isomorphism, and find
  a formula for $F^{-1}(x,y)$.
